planner: Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) system and sensors denied (MN-04) on 2026-10-01

merit: weak · The denial correctly applies the plan's terms to the documented facts. Criterion I.B of MP-DME-031 requires the member to be insulin-treated or to have documented problematic hypoglycemia. The record explicitly states the opposite on both points: metformin only, no insulin or sulfonylurea, and no glucose reading ever below 70 mg/dL. Diabetes is well controlled (A1c 6.6%). The CGM was ordered at the patient's request to see meal effects and support weight loss, which is a preference or wellness rationale, not a medical-necessity one. Missing documentation cannot be supplied truthfully, because the record affirmatively rules out the qualifying facts. Unless the plan's policy has an alternate pathway the denial overlooked, an appeal is very unlikely to succeed and the team should not build arguments that overstate the clinical picture.

strategy: Primary recommendation: tell the patient and clinic honestly that the denial appears to correctly apply MP-DME-031 criterion I.B, and steer them to the alternatives, especially an OTC CGM paid in cash or with HSA/FSA funds. If they still choose to appeal, keep it narrow and truthful. (1) Have the Policy Analyst confirm whether MP-DME-031 has any alternate pathway for non-insulin type 2 diabetes, such as a separate criterion, a diagnostic or professional CGM provision, or a pharmacy-benefit route. If one exists and the record genuinely meets it, argue under that pathway. (2) Check the denial for procedural defects: correct policy version, reviewer credentials, and whether a peer-to-peer was offered. (3) Do not claim insulin use, hypoglycemia, or poor control; the record contradicts all three. Any provider letter must reflect only what is actually true. (4) Note that external review is available, but evidence-based guidelines for non-insulin, well-controlled type 2 diabetes are unlikely to compel coverage.

discrepancy: No substantive discrepancy was found. The denial accurately paraphrases the current (01/01/2026) version of criterion I.B, including the 'any insulin' language. It does not apply the outdated pre-2026 requirement of three or more daily injections.

discrepancy: The denial cites only I.B. The record also lacks documentation for I.C (FDA-indication statement) and I.D (training). An appeal limited to I.B would not resolve these gaps, and the plan could raise them later.

discrepancy: Planner Q1: MP-DME-031 contains no alternative pathway. There is no provision for non-insulin, non-hypoglycemic type 2 diabetes, no trial period, and no short-term or diagnostic CGM pathway. Section I is the only coverage section; Section III states CGM is not medically necessary when Section I is not met.
discrepancy: Planner Q2: The criteria are conjunctive. 'ALL of the following' applies, with I.A AND I.B AND I.C AND I.D AND I.E. Within I.B, the two pathways are alternatives (B.1 OR B.2).

discrepancy: Planner Q3: 'Insulin-treated' means any insulin regimen, including a single daily basal dose; there is no injection-count minimum. 'Problematic hypoglycemia' means either recurrent level 2 events (<54 mg/dL) that persist despite multiple treatment adjustments, or at least one level 3 event requiring third-party assistance.

discrepancy: Planner Q5/Q6: The documents provided do not address professional or diagnostic CGM (CPT 95249/95250/95251), pharmacy-benefit coverage of sensors, or OTC CGM products. Whether any separate policy or formulary exists cannot be determined from these sources and would need to be requested from the plan.

merit: weak · Required criterion I.B is clearly not met by the documented facts. The note states no insulin, no sulfonylurea, and no glucose reading ever below 70 mg/dL, and the CGM was ordered at patient request for meal insight and weight loss. The denial quotes and applies the current (01/01/2026) policy accurately, so there is no misreading or outdated-criteria argument. Criteria I.C and I.D are also undocumented. The procedural defects in the notice do not create a coverage entitlement.

insurer would argue: Criterion I.B is mandatory and conjunctive with I.A–I.E, and the member concedes it is not met. MP-DME-031 Section III states CGM is not medically necessary when Section I is not met. Appeal reviewers apply the policy as written and have no authority to rewrite I.B on an individual appeal, so the denial is upheld on the member's own admission.

insurer would argue: The guideline-alignment argument fails. The 01/01/2026 revision postdates publication of the 2026 ADA Standards, which are released each December. The plan therefore had them in view and deliberately limited coverage to insulin use or problematic hypoglycemia. The 'any diabetes treatment where CGM helps' recommendation is Grade C, the lowest evidence grade, and the plan is not obligated to adopt every society recommendation.

insurer would argue: The member's A1c is 6.6%, already at goal and improving on metformin alone, with no hypoglycemia. A pooled 0.31-point A1c reduction is of marginal clinical value for a well-controlled patient, and nothing in the record shows CGM would change management. The plan is continue metformin and recheck in 6 months.
